description: MoonBunny is an ambitious space-tech team tackling the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. We're developing an interactive tool to explore lunar landing sites using orbital geometry, solar illumination, Earth visibility, and scientific visualization. We welcome curious problem-solvers with skills in Python, astrophysics, geospatial analysis, and software development. Our mission: turn complex lunar science into smarter exploration decisions.
summary:
**MoonBunny** is an interactive lunar landing-site analysis platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It addresses the challenge of evaluating solar illumination and direct-to-Earth communication opportunities at potential landing sites near the Moon's south pole.

Using NASA JPL Horizons ephemeris data and Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) topographic datasets, MoonBunny combines celestial positioning with preliminary terrain-horizon calculations to estimate when the Sun and Earth may be visible from selected lunar locations.

The platform features an interactive mission-control dashboard, solar and Earth elevation charts, adjustable observation periods, terrain-aware visibility estimates, and side-by-side site comparisons.

Our prototype analyzes two lunar south-pole sample locations using 721 hourly observations per site. Preliminary results demonstrate how local terrain can substantially change estimated sunlight and communication availability.

MoonBunny aims to make complex lunar mission-planning data more accessible to researchers, educators, students, and space enthusiasts while supporting transparent, data-driven exploration of potential landing-site trade-offs.
details:
MoonBunny — Lunar Landing Site Navigator

The Problem

Planning missions to the lunar south pole involves significant environmental challenges. Low solar elevation, crater-rim obstruction, and changing Earth visibility can influence the availability of solar energy and direct communication. Existing NASA scientific tools provide valuable information, but interpreting and comparing multiple landing-site scenarios can be difficult for non-specialists.

Our Solution

MoonBunny is a Python-based interactive web application designed to simplify preliminary lunar landing-site analysis.

The platform allows users to:

  • Explore two candidate lunar south-pole sample locations.
  • Compare solar illumination and potential Earth communication visibility.
  • Select observation periods within the available dataset.
  • Switch between ideal geometric and experimental terrain-aware horizon models.
  • Visualize Sun and Earth positions through interactive elevation charts and polar sky plots.
  • Examine visibility timelines and download scientific observation data.

NASA Data and Methodology

We used the NASA JPL Horizons System to obtain hourly Sun and Earth azimuth and elevation observations between November 14 and December 14, 2026.

We also used 5-meter-resolution NASA LOLA digital elevation models for Site 01 and Site 04 to investigate local terrain obstruction.

Our preliminary horizon calculations sampled terrain within a 5-kilometer radius at 5-degree azimuth intervals. The resulting horizon profiles were combined with Horizons observations to estimate whether the Sun and Earth appeared above the modeled terrain.

Preliminary Scientific Findings

For the selected observation period, our experimental terrain model produced the following results:

Site 01 — Connecting Ridge sample location

  • Potential solar visibility: 57.70%
  • Potential Earth visibility: 23.99%

Site 04 — Shackleton Rim sample location

  • Potential solar visibility: 41.61%
  • Potential Earth visibility: 0.00%

These percentages describe the proportion of hourly samples classified as visible under our preliminary model. They are not independently validated predictions of power generation or communication availability.

The comparison illustrates why lunar terrain may significantly affect site selection, even when the Sun or Earth appears above the ideal geometric horizon.

Technologies Used

  • Python for scientific calculations and application development
  • Streamlit for the interactive web dashboard
  • Pandas and NumPy for data processing
  • Plotly and Matplotlib for scientific visualization
  • Rasterio and PyProj for lunar terrain analysis and coordinate transformations
  • NASA JPL Horizons and LOLA datasets
  • GitHub for project source-code sharing
  • Google Colab and Visual Studio Code for development and testing

Innovation and Impact

MoonBunny brings lunar ephemeris observations and terrain-derived visibility estimates into one accessible interface. Rather than requiring users to interpret separate scientific datasets manually, the platform presents selected site and date comparisons through clear visualizations.

The approach can support educational exploration, early-stage mission concept studies, and greater public understanding of lunar environmental constraints.

Current Limitations and Future Development

MoonBunny is an experimental prototype, not a flight-qualified mission-planning system.

The current implementation uses precomputed observations for two sample locations, a limited 5-kilometer terrain search radius, and 5-degree azimuth sampling. Terrain coverage, observer-height conventions, reference systems, and the horizon methodology require further validation.

Future development could include more extensive terrain coverage, arbitrary landing-site coordinates, additional mission dates, higher-resolution horizon sampling, continuous communication-window calculations, and more detailed solar-power modeling.

Our vision is to make scientifically grounded lunar landing-site exploration faster, clearer, and more accessible.
